prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I have a perfect life. It isn't much, But it's enough for me. It keeps me alive And happy in a vague way: no disappointments On the near horizon, no pangs of doubt; Looking forward in anticipation, looking back In satisfaction at the conclusion of each day. I heed the promptings of my inner voice, And what I hear is comforting, full of reassurance For my own powers and innate superiority—the fake Security of someone in the grip of a delusion, In denial, climbing ever taller towers Like a tiny tyrant looking on his little kingdom With a secret smile, while all the while Time lies in wait. And what feels ample now Turns colorless and cold, and what seems beautiful And strong becomes an object of indifference Reaching out to no one, as later middle age Turns old, and the strength is gone. Right now the moments yield to me sweet Feelings of contentment, but the human Dies, and what I take for granted bears a name To be forgotten soon, as the things I know Turn into unfamiliar faces In a strange room, leaving merely A blank space, like a hole left in the wake Of a perfect life, which closes over.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker views their modest life as perfect because it provides safety, contentment, and freedom from immediate disappointment.
- Their confidence and sense of superiority offer reassurance but are ultimately portrayed as forms of delusion and denial.
- Time waits to erode what currently feels abundant, beautiful, and strong as middle age gives way to old age.
- Present contentment is temporary because physical strength, familiarity, and personal identity inevitably fade.
- Death and forgetting eventually erase the apparent permanence of a “perfect life,” leaving only a blank space that closes over.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem examines the illusion of a perfect, contented life through a reflective speaker whose self-assurance gradually confronts aging, decline, and mortality. It reveals that security, strength, identity, and memory inevitably fade, underscoring the transience of personal fulfillment and human existence.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: But, And, Looking

outputs.L1:
I have a perfect life. It isn’t much,  
but it is enough for me. It keeps me alive  
and vaguely happy: no disappointments  
on the near horizon, no pangs of doubt;  
looking forward with anticipation, looking back  
with satisfaction at the close of each day.

I heed the promptings of my inner voice,  
and what I hear is comforting, rich with reassurance  
of my own powers and innate superiority—the false  
security of someone in the grip of delusion,  
in denial, climbing ever-taller towers  
like a petty tyrant surveying his little kingdom  
with a secret smile, while all the while  
time lies in wait.

And what feels ample now  
turns colorless and cold, while what seems beautiful  
and strong becomes an object of indifference,  
reaching out to no one, as later middle age  
gives way to old age and strength is gone.

For now, the moments yield sweet  
feelings of contentment, but the human  
dies, and what I take for granted bears a name  
soon to be forgotten, as the things I know  
become unfamiliar faces  
in a strange room, leaving only  
a blank space, like a hole in the wake  
of a perfect life, closing over.
outputs.L2:
My life feels flawless. It may be modest, yet it gives me all I need, sustaining me and granting me a hazy kind of happiness. Nothing troubling appears close ahead; uncertainty causes no pain. I face the future with hope and end each day by viewing the past with contentment.

I follow the guidance within me, and its message is soothing, assuring me of my ability and natural greatness. But this confidence is counterfeit—the safety felt by a person trapped in illusion and refusing reality. I keep building higher, like a petty ruler gazing down upon his small domain with a concealed grin, unaware that time is patiently waiting.

Eventually, everything that now seems sufficient will become pale and lifeless. What appears powerful and lovely will inspire no feeling and connect with no one. Late middle age will give way to old age, and vigor will disappear.

For the present, each passing instant offers gentle contentment. Yet every person dies, and the identity I assume will soon be erased. Familiar things will become unknown faces surrounding me in an alien room. In the end, only emptiness will remain—a gap where this perfect life once existed, before even that opening seals itself.
outputs.L3:
The speaker regards their modest life as perfect because it offers safety, contentment, and protection from immediate disappointment. Their confidence, along with a subtle sense of superiority, provides comfort and reassurance. However, this attitude is ultimately presented as a form of delusion and denial, since it ignores the inevitability of change.

Time is already waiting to erode everything that currently seems abundant, beautiful, and strong. As middle age gives way to old age, physical strength will decline, familiar surroundings will change, and the speaker’s sense of identity will gradually weaken. The contentment they experience in the present is therefore only temporary, despite its apparent stability.

Ultimately, death and forgetting will destroy the illusion that any life can remain perfect or permanent. What once felt secure and complete will disappear, leaving only an absence—a blank space that eventually closes over, as though the speaker and their “perfect life” had never existed.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the illusion of a perfect and contented life through a speaker who initially appears confident in the stability of their world. The speaker takes comfort in personal security, physical strength, and a firmly established sense of identity, believing that these qualities provide lasting protection against uncertainty. This self-assurance creates an image of fulfillment: life seems complete, controlled, and resistant to change.

As the poem develops, however, this confidence begins to weaken. The speaker becomes increasingly aware of aging and physical decline, recognizing that strength and independence cannot be preserved forever. What once seemed permanent is revealed to be temporary. The body becomes more fragile, familiar sources of security lose their reliability, and the speaker’s belief in a settled, satisfying existence is gradually undermined.

The threat of loss extends beyond physical deterioration. Identity itself becomes unstable as memory begins to fade. The poem suggests that a person’s sense of self depends partly on the ability to remember experiences, relationships, and earlier versions of themselves. When memory declines, the continuity of the individual is placed at risk. The speaker must therefore confront not only death, but also the possibility of losing the qualities that make life meaningful before death arrives.

This gradual movement from confidence to vulnerability reveals the poem’s central irony. The speaker’s apparently perfect life cannot escape time, and the security they value is ultimately an illusion. Material comfort, personal strength, identity, and memory all remain subject to change and disappearance. By tracing this realization, the poem presents fulfillment as fragile rather than permanent. It ultimately emphasizes the transience of human existence, reminding readers that even the most secure and satisfying life is shaped by aging, loss, and mortality.
outputs.L5: I kept looking for the right path, but every road seemed uncertain. And then I realized: sometimes moving forward matters more than knowing exactly where you are going.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about someone who believes they have a perfect life but gradually realizes that aging, death, and oblivion will erase everything they value.
counterfactuals.output:
Every morning, the curtains opened  
on the same obedient light.

The floorboards held their polish.  
The kettle knew its small song.  
Photographs stood in silver frames—  
wedding, children, summer water—  
each moment caught  
before it could become another.

In the garden, roses climbed  
the measured trellis.  
The house was paid for.  
The locks were sound.  
Friends arrived carrying wine  
and left with laughter  
still warm in the rooms.

What more could a life be  
but this arrangement of beloved things,  
this table set for six,  
this name written neatly  
on envelopes and deeds?

Then one day the mirror  
failed to agree.

A pale thread crossed the hair.  
A hand, lifting a cup,  
seemed briefly to belong  
to someone farther away.

The children’s faces sharpened  
into strangers who resembled them.  
The dog slept longer.  
A chair remained empty  
after winter.

Still, the roses climbed.

Years loosened the roof tiles,  
blurred the ink in old letters.  
Voices once summoned at will  
grew difficult to hear.  
Names slipped their hooks  
and sank beneath conversation.

The house, too, began to forget:  
a crack along the plaster,  
a door swollen in its frame,  
dust practicing its quiet claim  
on every shelf.

At night, awake beside a breathing body,  
they understood the terrible arithmetic:

that love does not prevent an ending,  
that memory is only a room  
inside a mortal head,  
that even grief will someday lose  
the face it mourns.

The photographs would fade.  
The children would age.  
The garden would become  
another garden,  
then weeds,  
then earth without a boundary.

And the name—  
so carefully signed,  
so often spoken—  
would thin in the mouths of descendants,  
be misspelled in a record,  
be read once by a stranger,  
then not at all.

Morning came anyway.

The kettle sang  
its one bright, foolish song.  
Light entered without mercy  
and touched each doomed possession  
as if blessing it:

the cup,  
the ring,  
the table scarred by years,  
the sleeping hand nearby.

For a moment, everything was perfect—

not because it would remain,

but because it would not.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a melancholy contemporary poem that begins with “I have a perfect life” and shifts from quiet contentment to existential dread.
counterfactuals.output:
I have a perfect life—  
the kettle clicks itself quiet,  
rain beads on the window  
like a careful thought.

Someone I love is sleeping  
in the next room.  
Their shoes wait by the door,  
faithful as small animals.

The bills are paid.  
The basil leans toward morning.  
My phone glows with weather,  
then goes dark in my hand.

Nothing is wrong.  
This is what frightens me.

Beyond the glass, the city  
keeps all its windows lit,  
each room holding a person  
who believes they are inside time.

I listen to the pipes cool.  
I listen to the elevator  
carry no one I can see  
past floor after floor.

Someday the cups will remain  
but not our mouths.  
The bed will keep its shape  
for less than an hour.

Even now, beneath the ordinary—  
the clean plate, the folded towel—  
something vast is opening  
without sound, without hurry,

and every beautiful thing I have  
is already becoming  
the last time  
I will ever see it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a first-person poem exploring complacency, self-delusion, middle age, mortality, and the fear of being forgotten.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Comfortable Chair**

I have mistaken stillness for peace,  
the locked door for a settled house,  
the dust for proof that nothing leaves.

Each morning, I polish the same small lies:  
there will be time,  
I am not afraid,  
my life is waiting just beyond  
this week, this winter, this tiredness.

The mirror has begun to tell the truth  
in silver syllables at my temples,  
in the soft surrender of the jaw.  
I call it character. I call it weather.  
I do not call it what it is.

At noon, I sit in my comfortable chair  
while the sun moves without me.  
I praise myself for having arrived,  
though I cannot name the country,  
though all my luggage is unopened.

Somewhere, the young man I was  
is still making extravagant promises.  
I hear him through the walls sometimes,  
laughing at caution, spending years  
as if the purse could never empty.

I want to warn him.  
I want to become him.  
Instead, I turn the page,  
refill the glass,  
let evening gather like a verdict.

Death is not the dark that frightens me,  
but the room afterward:  
my name fading from the mouths I loved,  
my face misplaced in an unlabeled drawer,  
the world continuing with terrible ease.

So I leave these words—  
not brave, not wise,  
only fingerprints upon the glass.

I was here, I tell the dark.  
I was here.

And the dark, patient as always,  
does not disagree.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a reflective literary monologue in verse about a person enjoying an ordinary, satisfying life while time silently waits to strip it away.
counterfactuals.output:
I wake before the kettle’s little cry  
and stand barefoot where the floor is cold.  
The window gathers morning by degrees—  
a pale coin laid upon the table,  
the sparrows stitching noise into the hedge.

Nothing is remarkable, and this  
is what I love: the chipped blue cup,  
the chair that knows the shape of me,  
bread opening its warm, familiar heart  
beneath the patient knife.

At noon I walk the same small road.  
The grocer lifts his hand. A dog  
pulls someone laughing toward the park.  
Clouds pass without explanation.  
I buy two pears, a paper, thyme.

There are evenings when the rooms grow gold  
and every common thing forgives the world:  
the folded towel, the lamp’s low pool,  
a coat asleep behind the door,  
your voice arriving from another room.

I have not asked for trumpets.  
Let others chase the bright, receding train.  
I have this soup, this rain against the glass,  
this book gone soft from being read,  
this bed where two breaths rise and fall.

Yet somewhere—never hurried, never seen—  
Time sits quietly with its hands unclosed.  
It does not knock. It does not need to.  
It watches dust turn slowly in the sun  
and knows the names of everything I keep.

One day it will begin with little thefts:  
a face misplaced, a stair grown steep,  
the garden yielding fewer summer bees.  
Then walls, then hands, then even grief—  
all borrowed things called gently home.

But not tonight.

Tonight the kettle sings.  
You set the plates. I strike a match.  
Outside, the dark leans close and listens  
while we speak of nothing worth remembering—  
and I remember all of it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a somber free-verse meditation on the false security of happiness, using imagery of a tiny tyrant, a fading kingdom, unfamiliar faces, and a hole that eventually closes over.
counterfactuals.output:
We called it happiness  
because it fit inside the hand—  
a warm coin,  
a small bright despot  
ordering the hours to kneel.

We obeyed.

Beyond the window,  
the kingdom thinned into evening:  
towers losing their names,  
gardens surrendering color,  
roads carrying everyone away.

At the table, unfamiliar faces  
wore the eyes of those we loved.  
They spoke gently,  
as if gentleness could bar the door  
against winter.

But joy was never a fortress.  
It was a lamp in an abandoned room,  
burning down without witness.

Even grief, which seemed bottomless,  
was only a hole in the earth.

Rain entered.  
Leaves entered.  
Years leaned over it.

And slowly, without mercy or promise,  
the ground closed over.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
